content_voiceover: This slide walks through a real local case that became a transfusion dispute, a good illustration of ABO discrepancy. A patient with a preceding cold illness developed weakness, chills, jaundice, tachycardia, and fever, then became agitated and somnolent within an hour, with no transfusion given before resuscitation began. Hemoglobin was critically low at 4.4 grams per deciliter, and blood was urgently cross-matched. But the blood bank hesitated to release units, all four typing runs showed AB positive, yet the family insisted the patient was actually type A. The antibody screen was positive against both screening cells, and the serum was incompatible with eight AB units and with both A and O stock units. Simulated results showed strong reactions everywhere, Anti-A 4 plus, Anti-B 3 plus, Anti-D 4 plus, and both A and B reverse cells at 4 plus. The lesson, an extremely potent cold agglutinin distorted both forward and reverse ABO typing at once, a true ABO discrepancy that can dangerously delay transfusion if not recognized.
keypoints: Severe anemia, hemoglobin 4.4, urgent transfusion need, but blood bank hesitant to release
Forward typing repeatedly showed AB positive; family reported the patient was type A
Both forward and reverse typing abnormal defines a true ABO discrepancy
Antibody screen positive and multiple cross-matches incompatible, a classic strong cold agglutinin picture
Delayed recognition of cold agglutinin interference risks dangerous transfusion delay in critical anemia
keypoint_voiceover: Key takeaway, severe anemia with a critical hemoglobin needs urgent transfusion, but repeated AB positive typing conflicted with the family's report of type A. Both forward and reverse typing were abnormal, that combination defines a true ABO discrepancy, here caused by an extremely strong cold agglutinin. Recognizing this quickly is essential, because delayed release of blood in a critically anemic patient can be life threatening.
